voiceover: You know this verse. Watch the order. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Start with the verb. The Word was in the beginning. When John describes created things a few lines down, he uses a verb that means came to be — began, started. Of the Word in the beginning he writes a different verb: was. Already there. The Word did not begin when the beginning began. When the beginning happened, the Word already was. And three lines later: all things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. That puts the Word on the Maker's side of the line between Creator and creation — not among the things made. Now the order. John could have written simply that the Word was God, and stopped. Instead he says first that the Word was with God, and only then that the Word was God — two claims set side by side, not collapsed into one. So the Word is personally distinct from the Father, and fully shares the one divine nature. God is one, yet there is real relationship within his own life. Two truths, held together, not one traded away for the other. And then John writes the line everything has been building toward: the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us. So when John says "the Word," he means Jesus of Nazareth — the eternal self-expression of God became a particular man you could touch, walk beside, and eat with.
